rashi:a1.1: And they redeem at any time: if they sold a field, they redeem it immediately, whereas an Israelite is not permitted to redeem it in less than two years, as it is written: “According to the number of years of the crops he shall sell to you” (Leviticus 25:15).
rashi:a1.2: Granted that they are not included in the release of land: that is, in the whole law of the release of land, for we learned: [Priests and Levites] sell at any time.
tosafot:a1.1: And they redeem at any time: if they sold a field they redeem it immediately, whereas an Israelite is not permitted to redeem in less than two years, as it is written: “According to the number of years of the crops,” etc. Granted that they are not included in the release of land: that is, in the whole law of the release of land, for we learned: “And they sell at any time.” So far the commentary [of Rashi]. In Rosh HaShana (29a) Rashi does not have the reading “granted that they are not included in the release of land,” because it implies that [the field] does not return to the priests in the Jubilee, and that is not so; here, however, he explained it well. And it is somewhat difficult: what does the release of money have to do with the Jubilee? For it is taught in the Sifrei: “In this year of Jubilee” (Leviticus 25:13): this [year] sets slaves free, and the Sabbatical Year does not set slaves free. [One might argue] a fortiori that the Jubilee releases [debts]: if the Sabbatical Year, which does not set slaves free, releases [debts], is it not logical that the Jubilee, which does set slaves free, releases [debts]? The verse states: “And this is the manner of the release” (Deuteronomy 15:2): the Sabbatical Year releases [debts], and the Jubilee does not. Evidently the Jubilee does not release money. One can say, though, that the release of money is somewhat connected to the Jubilee, since the Sabbatical Year is in effect only when the Jubilee is in effect. [On 4a:] “And this eating of sacrificial meat is for atonement, as it is written: ‘And they shall eat those things with which atonement was made,’ etc.: this teaches that the priests eat and the owners achieve atonement; one might say no zimmun is required, etc. They join together: if one priest, one Levite and one Israelite ate, a priest can eat non-sacred food together with a non-priest; therefore they join.” So far the commentary. From here it would appear that three people who are forbidden by vow to benefit from one another do not join [for a zimmun], since none of them can eat with his fellow. Yet it seems that this is not a clear proof for three people under such a vow, since teruma is different: it has no permission for a non-priest even by asking [a Sage to release the vow], which is not so for one forbidden by vow to benefit. I discussed this at length in Berakhot (45a).
gershom:a1.1: And they redeem at any time: as is explained there.
gershom:a2.1: It teaches us: that they are included in the mitzvot of Rosh HaShana. What is the reason? Even though they are not included in the release of land, they are included in the release of money and in sending away slaves, as [other] Jews are.
rashi:a3.1: And this eating of sacrificial meat is for atonement, as it is written: “And they shall eat those things with which atonement was made,” which teaches that the priests eat and the owners achieve atonement (Yoma 68b). [So] one might say it does not require a zimmun; it teaches us, etc.
gershom:a3.1: “And they shall eat those things with which atonement was made”: this teaches that the priests eat and the owners achieve atonement. So this eating is an obligation, and it should not require a zimmun. It teaches us: “And you shall eat and be satisfied”: the Merciful One made it depend on being satisfied, and that is present here.
rashi:a5.1: They join, etc.: if one priest, one Levite and one Israelite ate. A priest can eat non-sacred food together with a non-priest; therefore they join.
gershom:a4.1: It is necessary only where the priests are eating teruma: two priests, and one non-priest eating non-sacred food.
rashi:a7.1: It is necessary only according to ben Bukhri: Rava’s statement is explained at the end of the discussion.
rashi:a7.2: Who contributes: the shekels [collected from] the first of Adar.
rashi:a7.3: Is not a sinner: as is explained below, that it is not [bringing] a non-sacred item into the courtyard, even though he is not obligated ab initio, as it is written: “For everyone that passed over to those who were counted” (Exodus 38:26), and the tribe of Levi was not counted.
gershom:a5.1: Any priest who contributes: brings the half-shekel for the collection of the chamber.
gershom:a6.1: Is not a sinner: and if he does not contribute he is not a sinner, for the choice is his.
tosafot:a7.1: Any priest who does not contribute is a sinner: for he expounds “This they shall give” (Exodus 30:13): twelve tribes [shall give], as the numerical value of zeh [this] is twelve. He could equally have said: Any Levite who does not contribute [is a sinner]; but [he spoke of priests] because [of Levites] he could not say “because they interpret this verse for themselves.”
rashi:a8.1: But the priests interpret this verse for themselves: for their own benefit, and not in accordance with the law.
gershom:a7.1: They interpret this verse: for their own benefit, to exempt [themselves] from the shekels.
rashi:a9.1: It is ours: for they come from the collection of the chamber, and if we contribute to the chamber, the omer meal offering, the two loaves and the shewbread turn out to be ours; how then can they be eaten? It is written: “It shall not be eaten.” But we do not accept this exposition, for “It shall be wholly made to smoke” is written about the meal offering of priests alone; with a communal meal offering, follow the majority.
gershom:a8.1: They are ours: since they come from the collection of the chamber, how could we eat of them?
gershom:a9.1: And according to ben Bukhri [the printed text reads “ben Kovdi”]: why did he say he is not a sinner? Since he is not obligated, he is bringing a non-sacred item into the courtyard: those offerings bought with their shekels.
rashi:a10.1: Who transfers it to the community, etc.: and therefore, according to ben Bukhri, who exempts priests from the shekels, the mishna was needed to teach that a priest who valuated himself or another gives the valuation like an Israelite. For it might enter your mind, etc.; it teaches us (that they are not derived [from one another]).
gershom:a10.1: That they transfer them to the community: those shekels, as a gift to the community; otherwise they could not bring them.
rashi:a12.1: Should not be less than a sela: for a poor person in valuations is judged by what he can afford, as it is written: “According to the means of the one who vowed” (Leviticus 27:8), etc., and he never gives less than a sela, as is said in the second chapter (below, 7b): there is no valuation of less than a sela, and the reason given there is from this verse. Since [the verse] comes for that, it would not enter one’s mind to use it for another exposition, to exempt priests from valuations, and the mishna would not have been needed.
gershom:a11.1: Abaye said to him: This verse, “And all your valuations,” does not come for this; it comes for that: that all the valuations you assess should not be less than a shekel. For if a person valuated his fellow and cannot afford to give a shekel, he gives nothing; but if he later became rich, he pays his full valuation. But if he could afford to give a shekel and gave it, then even if he became rich afterward he gives no more.
rashi:a13.1: Priests were exempted from redeeming the firstborn son in the first chapter of Bekhorot (4a), by an a fortiori inference: if they exempted those of the Israelites in the wilderness, all the more so their own.
gershom:a12.1: Rather, Abaye said it was necessary: to say “priests,” for it might enter your mind, etc.
rashi:a14.1: So too they should not be included in the ram of the guilt offering: but they are Jews! Rather, certainly we do not expound this way; and still, why does the mishna need to teach “priests, Levites and Israelites”?
gershom:a13.1: Rava said to him: If so, with regard to the ram of the guilt offering, [as it is written: “And he shall bring his guilt offering to the Lord, a ram without blemish from the flock, according to your valuation in silver shekels”], let us likewise say: since it juxtaposed valuations to the guilt offering, anyone who is included in valuations is included in the ram of the guilt offering.
rashi:a15.1: Then he shall be set before the priest: a poor man who valuated himself or another.
rashi:a15.2: But not a priest before a priest: so a priest would not be included in valuations, for if he is poor, “Then he shall be set before the priest” cannot be said of him. The mishna teaches us [otherwise].
gershom:a14.1: [Rather, Rava said: It was necessary to teach “priests,” for it might enter your mind that it means] an Israelite before a priest, since it is written in the section: “Speak to the children of Israel” (Leviticus 27:2).
gershom:a15.1: It teaches us: that priests too are included in “Israel.”
rashi:a16.1: Are valuated, to add, etc.: that is, the Master said above: Everyone is valuated, to add a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils.
rashi:a17.1: An unspecified valuation: it is explained below, and the whole baraita is explained below.
gershom:a16.1: An unspecified valuation: explained [below]. [The printed text is garbled here; the editor suggests it should read: below, at “The Master said,” the whole baraita is explained.]
rashi:a17.2: The valuation of his limbs: if he said, “The valuation of my hand is upon me,” he has said nothing, for there is no valuation for limbs. But if he said, “The assessment of my hand is upon me,” he gives the value of his hand.
tosafot:a17.1: He gives the valuation of all of him and does not give the valuation of limbs: [This needed a verse,] for it might enter one’s mind to include [the limb, i.e., to make him pay], because a person knows that limbs have no valuation, so he must have meant all of his limbs together. It teaches us [otherwise]. One can also say: it might enter one’s mind that since limbs are subject to assessment, they are also subject to valuation.
gershom:a17.1: He gives the valuation of all of him: where he said, “My valuation is upon me.”
rashi:a18.1: On which the soul depends: if he said, “The valuation of my head” or “the valuation of my liver.”
rashi:a18.2: The verse states: “Persons”: the Merciful One made it depend on the soul, and if he valuated a part on which the soul depends, he gives the valuation of all of him.
gershom:a18.1: And he does not give the valuation of his limbs: as we learned: [If he said,] “The valuation of my hand” or “the valuation of my foot is upon me,” he has said nothing. But if he valuated a limb on which the soul depends, such as his head or his heart, he must give the valuation of all of him, because it is written: “According to your valuation of persons.”
rashi:a18.3: And not the dead: if he said, “The valuation of this dead person is upon me,” he has said nothing.
tosafot:a18.1: “Persons,” and not the dead: even though [a corpse] is forbidden for benefit by Torah law and has no assessed value, it might enter one’s mind that it is included in valuations, since a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils, who have no assessed value, were included.
gershom:a19.1: “Persons,” and not the dead: you valuate one whose soul is in him, and you do not valuate the dead.
rashi:a19.1: Then he shall be set and he shall value: this is written about a poor man who valuated.
tosafot:a19.1: And I should not exclude a moribund person; the verse states: “Then he shall be set and he shall value”: And if you say: but in the second chapter of Ḥullin (30a), [an animal in which] one cut both [signs], or most of both, and it is still convulsing, is [said to be] within the category of setting and valuing! One can say that an animal has more vitality and can stand; and it mentions “convulsing” only because [then] it is not yet a carcass. And this requires examination: the plain sense of “Then he shall be set… and shall value” refers to the one who vows, for that verse says: “According to the means of the one who vowed shall [the priest] value him”; and a moribund person can vow and valuate, as we learned in tractate Semaḥot. So from where do we derive, from “Then he shall be set,” which in that verse refers to the one who valuates, that [a moribund person] is not valuated?
gershom:a20.1: And a moribund person is not within [the category of] setting.
rashi:a20.1: Alternatively, “persons”: why is it stated? For had it not said “persons” but “person,” I would say I have only one who valuated one, as it is written: “When a man shall clearly utter [a vow], according to your valuation of persons” (Leviticus 27:2), which would mean one who valuated one.
tosafot:a20.1: From where [do we know] one who valuated a hundred: for example, he said, “The valuation of so-and-so and so-and-so and so-and-so is upon me,” saying “valuation” in the singular; it might enter one’s mind that it is not a valuation. It teaches us [that it is].
rashi:a20.2: Another explanation of “persons”: why is it stated? For had it said “person,” I would say I have only a man who valuated, whether a man or a woman, as it is written: “When a man shall clearly utter… persons,” which implies that the man valuates any soul whatsoever.
rashi:b3.1: “Persons”: for this is what “according to your valuation of persons” implies: all persons can be valuated.
rashi:b4.1: And anyone who is not included in valuations: such as a tumtum and a hermaphrodite, for “the male” is written, which implies a definite male [and] a definite female.
gershom:b1.1: To include a tumtum and a hermaphrodite in assessments: that they can be the object of a vow, and a person can say, “His assessment is upon me.”
gershom:b2.1: The verse states “Then shall be”: from “then shall be” it includes them in assessments, so that they are subject to assessment; and from “your valuation shall be for the male… and if it be a female” it excludes them from valuations.
rashi:b7.1: An unspecified valuation: he did not say, “My valuation is upon me,” nor “The valuation of so-and-so is upon me,” but said, “A valuation is upon me.”
rashi:b7.2: Three shekels: as it is written: “And for the female three shekels” (Leviticus 27:6), and this is the smallest of the valuations.
tosafot:b7.1: And how much is the smallest of the valuations? Three shekels: even though it says in the Tosefta of our tractate: “[One who says,] ‘A valuation is upon me,’ unspecified, brings the smallest. And how much is the smallest? Five sela’im,” one can say that there it means an unspecified valuation of a male.
rashi:b8.1: If you grasped a lot, you did not grasp: for one can object: grasp the small amount.
rashi:b8.2: If you grasped a little, you grasped: for if someone objects to you, “Grasp the large amount,” he does not disagree with your words but adds to them, since the small amount is included in the large one.
gershom:b3.1: If you grasped a lot, you did not grasp: for one could say [grasp] the little.
gershom:b4.1: If you grasped a little, you grasped: for even if someone says “a lot,” you have grasped [it], since the little is included in the lot, and he does not contradict your words.
rashi:b9.1: With regard to affordability: that if he is poor and “too poor for your valuation,” the priest shall not value him at less than a shekel. But under the law of a fixed valuation, none is less than three shekels.
gershom:b5.1: It is written with regard to affordability: [as we said] above.
rashi:b10.1: But the verse, “according to your valuation,” what does it come for? Since an unspecified valuation is only three shekels, even without the verse I would know that he is not exempt with nothing, and less than this he could not give, for no fixed valuation is less than this.
gershom:b6.1: But why do I need the verse? Since from “you grasped a little” we learn [that it is] the smallest of the valuations, why do I need “according to your valuation”?
rashi:b10.2: That he is not judged by affordability: that even if he cannot afford three shekels, he gives three shekels.
gershom:b7.1: To say that he is not judged by affordability: that if he has only a shekel, he does not give it and become exempt from then on; rather, he is obligated in the full valuation, because it is as though he specified three shekels.
rashi:b10.3: It is as though he specified: since he said, “An unspecified valuation is upon me,” and he knows that the smallest of the valuations is three shekels, it is like one who said, “Three shekels are upon me.” It is not like one who says, “My valuation is upon me” or “The valuation of so-and-so is upon me,” for there the matter is not evident, since not everyone knows a person’s age; but here it is plain, for he did not attach it to any person.
tosafot:b10.1: To say that he is not judged by affordability: What is the reason? It is as though he specified. “Since he said, ‘An unspecified valuation is upon me,’ and he knows that the smallest of the valuations is three shekels, it is like one who said, ‘Three shekels are upon me.’ It is not like one who says, ‘The valuation of so-and-so,’ for there the matter is not evident, since not everyone knows his age; but here it is plain, for he did not attach it to any person.” So far the commentary [of Rashi]. And it is difficult: when he says, “The valuation of so-and-so is upon me,” he knows that [the person] is not [under] a month old, so he is obligated [at least] five sela’im, and yet he is judged by affordability, [paying] one sela or two. It seems [better] to explain “as though he specified” as being like one who says explicitly, “Three sela’im are upon me,” since he said an unspecified valuation. For certainly, if he said, “The valuation of so-and-so, who is twenty,” even though he knows he will be obligated fifty sela’im, nevertheless, since he attached the valuation to the one valuated, it is a decree of the Torah that he be judged by affordability; and it is not like one who specifies, “Fifty sela’im are upon me for Temple maintenance.”
rashi:b11.1: There are those who say that Rav Naḥman said: the verse comes to say that it is called a valuation, its law is like that of other valuations, and it is judged by affordability.
gershom:b8.1: There are those who say, etc.
rashi:b11.2: Obvious: for how is it different from other valuations?
gershom:b9.1: Obvious: for he said an unspecified valuation, and it is fit to be judged by affordability.
rashi:b12.1: Read into it “valuation” and “according to your valuation”: it could have written “valuation,” and that would teach the unspecified valuation; since it wrote “according to your valuation,” this too is to be expounded.
tosafot:b12.1: Read into it “valuation” and “according to your valuation”: [it is expounded] from the extra [form] “according to your valuation,” for it could have written “valuation”; it expounds from what is extra, while “valuation” itself is needed.
rashi:b16.1: As we are about to state: to include a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils.
gershom:b10.1: Lest you say, etc.: as we are about to say below, that it is needed for a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils.
rashi:b19.1: But you have derived these from it: one who valuated a hundred, and a woman who valuated.
gershom:b11.1: But you derived [“persons”] for these: for “I have only one who valuated one,” etc., and for a woman who valuated, etc.
rashi:b20.1: It is equivalent: even if “person” were written, they would all follow from it: a part on which the soul depends, one who valuated a hundred, and a woman who valuated. For “person” [nefesh] implies a woman, and implies many persons, as it says: “And persons [nefesh adam], of the women, sixteen thousand” (Numbers 31 [the count of sixteen thousand is in verse 40]). And even though from a single “person” we could not draw three expositions, they would all come, since they are equivalent and equal and all derivable from this verse; you cannot establish one exposition more than another, so which of them would you exclude? Therefore they all come from it, and “persons” is needed for a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils, so that you not exclude them from a vow of valuation.
rashi:b20.2: Equivalent [shakul]: equal. For all the expositions are equally derivable from this verse, and none has more weight than another, that we should say this one alone is included; they are equivalent. There is a similar case in Bava Kamma (3a), in the first discussion.
gershom:b12.1: These do not need a verse, for it is equivalent [and they all come]: that is, from where we derive that one valuates [one], from “When a man shall clearly utter [according to your valuation],” these too are equivalent to be derived from “man.” For what difference is there to me between one who valuated one and one who valuated a hundred? Just as when one valuated one his valuation is consecrated, so too when he valuated a hundred. And just as a man valuates [a man], so a woman valuates, for the Torah made a woman equal to a man. A part on which the soul depends comes from “person,” and the dead and the moribund come from “then he shall be set.”
gershom:b13.1: “Persons” is left over for a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils.
rashi:b21.1: For assessments: for if it is not relevant for valuations, since we need a definite male, apply it to assessments.
rashi:b22.1: That he is assessed by its significance: that all of him is assessed by one limb on which his significance depends; if he said, “The assessment of my head is upon me,” he gives the assessment of all of him.
gershom:b14.1: To say that he is assessed by the significance of the limb: that if he said, “The assessment of one limb is upon me,” he is assessed according to the importance of the limb: if it is a limb on which the soul depends, he is assessed by the value of all of him; and if not, he has said nothing.
rashi:b23.1: This is the reading: It might enter your mind to say: “A vow according to your valuation of persons” is written; [so] anyone who is included in valuations is assessed by its significance, even when he said, “The assessment of my head is upon me,” and anyone who is not included in valuations, when he said, “The assessment of my head is upon me,” is not assessed by its significance, since “persons” is written in connection with valuation. It teaches us [otherwise].
rashi:b24.1: They appraise between them: how much it is worth, and they divide its value. And I am uncertain why it says “partners” there and “appraise” here.
tosafot:b24.1: He and the Temple are partners, etc.: the commentary explains that with consecration it speaks of partnership, to say that he and the Temple share, for one who consecrates does so generously; but with a sale “appraise” fits, a term of appraisal: that is, they appraise the limb he sold, for what work it is fit, and he takes according to its value. [Rashi on our page instead says he is unsure why the two terms differ.]
gershom:b15.1: He and the Temple are partners in it: that is, since its head is consecrated and the body is his, and he cannot separate the head from the body, both are partners in it. They cannot sell it and divide its value because of the Temple’s share, for the prohibition of misusing consecrated property applies to it.
gershom:b16.1: They appraise between them: since it is non-sacred, they sell [it] and divide its value, or one of them buys out his fellow’s share.
rashi:b25.1: And Rav Pappa said: what is the reason that with a cow he consecrated only its head?
rashi:b25.2: Because the head of an ox is sold at the butcher’s: but it is not customary to sell the head of a slave or the head of a donkey; therefore he sold half of it, [or] consecrated half of it.
gershom:b17.1: The Temple has only its head: since it is customary to sell an animal’s head, without the body, at the butcher shops.
rashi:b26.1: And is not assessed by its significance: for it teaches, “He and the Temple are partners in it,” and it does not all belong to the Temple.
tosafot:b26.1: But a cow and a donkey, which are not included in valuations, are not assessed by its significance: and all the more so, when one consecrates the body, the sanctity spreads to all of it.
gershom:b18.1: And is not assessed by its significance: for it does not all become consecrated, even though the soul depends on the head.
rashi:b26.2: But a slave, who is included in valuations: as taught in the mishna; and this baraita teaches about a slave too, “He and the Temple are partners in it,” so he is not assessed by its significance.
rashi:b27.1: Rather, it is not difficult: this baraita is about items consecrated for the altar, where he said, “The head of this donkey” or “this slave is for the value of a burnt offering,” and it is not assessed by its significance, for when “persons” is written, it is written with regard to valuations, which are consecrated for Temple maintenance. And when we say that it is assessed by its significance, even a tumtum, it is where he vowed his assessment for Temple maintenance.
tosafot:b27.1: This is not difficult: this is with items consecrated for the altar, that is with items consecrated for Temple maintenance: the baraita is about items consecrated for the altar, where he said, “The head of the donkey is consecrated for the value of a burnt offering,” and it is not assessed by its significance, for when “persons” is written it is written about valuations, which are consecrated for Temple maintenance. And when we say that it is assessed by its significance, even a tumtum, it is where he vows his assessment for Temple maintenance.
gershom:b19.1: This is with items consecrated for the altar, etc.: that is, where it says the two of them are partners, it is where he consecrated it with the sanctity of the altar.
gershom:b20.1: And where he consecrated it with the sanctity of Temple maintenance, it is assessed by its significance, which is like valuations, which have the sanctity of Temple maintenance.
rashi:b28.1: Let the sanctity spread through all of it: since it is fit to be sacrificed.
